summary:
Arequipa department has no region-specific trans law, ordinance, incident series or enforcement finding on record. All three attached sources are national in scope, and as national measures they bind the department. The operative legal frame for a visitor to Arequipa is Peru's national one.

Peru does not criminalise trans identity, but the national Congress has legislated against trans people's use of public facilities, hate-crime protection for LGBT people has been removed from the Penal Code, and recorded violence against trans women is rising.

The facility restriction is in force. On 20 February 2025 the Commission on Women and Family approved unanimously, for plenary debate, the dictamen covering bills 6506 and 8457, which bar entry to public sanitary facilities destined for the sex opposite to one's birth sex, with exceptions for custody, medical care or accompanying an adult, a child under 12 or a disabled person, and which require unambiguous signage; as of that date the dictamen still awaited plenary backing. The Congress plenary then approved on 2 April 2025, exempt from a second vote, the law 'fortaleciendo el derecho a la indemnidad sexual de los niños y adolescentes', whose article 5 bars anyone whose biological sex does not match the facility's intended sex from public sanitary facilities, with exceptions limited to accompanying or assisting minors, patients or people with specific needs. The same legislative package bans inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

Hate-crime protection for LGBT people is absent from the Penal Code. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures.

Recorded violence is rising and trans women bear the largest share. The TLGBI Rights Observatory's annual report counts 54 killings of TLGBI people and 170 rights-violation cases in Peru between 2020 and 2023, with hate crimes increasing. In February 2023 the trans woman Rubí Torres Silvano, aged 31, was kidnapped in central Lima and murdered in Carabayllo with approximately 30 gunshots by the 'Los Gallegos' gang; the bodies showed gunshots, stab wounds and throat-slitting that indicate extreme hate.
tangentialFactors:
The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. The bathroom provisions adopted in April 2025 sit in direct tension with that standard.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte of 15 April 2025, finds that article 5 implicitly brands trans people as more prone to entering bathrooms to harass or sexually abuse minors, conditions basic rights on verifiable 'biological sex', and violates equality, non-discrimination and gender self-determination. The same analysis records that Congress had already banned inclusive language and again rejected equal marriage.

The 2017 repeal left Peru one of only three countries in South America, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments are on record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people, in reference to the vague child-protection articles of the April 2025 law.
localsOnly:
Enforcement of the facility restriction reaches private premises. A consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy.

Trans-rights activist Gianna Camacho, quoted on the February 2025 dictamen, warned that the measure is discriminatory and that security staff would effectively judge people by personal criteria, such as requesting their DNI.

Hostility has been voiced from official and media platforms. The IDEHPUCP analysis records dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three to four years.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory records a trans-specific incident, arrest, refusal of service or facilities dispute inside Arequipa department. Whether article 5 has been invoked by security staff, police or premises in Arequipa is not sourced here, and the enforcement examples available (the gym complaint, the television harassment) occurred elsewhere in Peru.

The 2020 to 2023 figures are national totals for Peru and are not disaggregated by department, so the share of recorded killings or violations occurring in Arequipa is unresolved.

Gianna Camacho, co-author of the 2024 hate-crime reporting, states that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry, so the true scale of violence is higher than the counts cited.

The bills 6506 and 8457 contain no Arequipa-specific provision; their application in the department follows from their status as national law rather than from any local implementing act, and no local implementing act is sourced.
